unit.title: Reform & Civic Action Study Tool
unit.subtitle: How have everyday people made change? Learn the vocabulary, study the reformers, and build your own Civic Action Product.
unit.essentialQuestion: How have everyday people made change — and how will you?

vocabulary.definition: The period from roughly 1890 to 1920 when Americans organized to fix problems caused by industrialization, urbanization, and political corruption
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: America around 1900 had huge problems — unsafe food, child labor, corrupt politicians — and a generation of people decided to stop complaining and start fixing. Their playbook is the one we'll study, because it still works.
vocabulary.example: During the Progressive Era, reformers won laws on food safety, workplace conditions, and voting rights within a single generation
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Progressive Era was the period from about 1890 to 1920 when Americans organized to fix the problems of industrialization and corruption. Reformers exposed abuses, built movements, and pushed new laws through government. Their strategies became a playbook that later movements have used ever since.

vocabulary.definition: A journalist of the Progressive Era who investigated and exposed corruption, dangerous conditions, and abuse to push the public toward reform
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Reporters who dug through the muck — the ugly stuff powerful people wanted hidden — and published it. Their stories made readers so angry that change became impossible to ignore.
vocabulary.example: Upton Sinclair was a muckraker whose novel The Jungle exposed the meatpacking industry and helped pass food safety laws
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A muckraker was a Progressive Era journalist who exposed corruption and dangerous conditions to the public. Writers like Upton Sinclair and photographers like Jacob Riis made hidden problems impossible to ignore. Their work shows that gathering and publishing evidence is itself a form of civic action.

vocabulary.definition: A change made to fix a problem in society, usually through new laws, rules, or practices
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Not tearing the system down and not leaving it alone — fixing it. Reform means identifying what's broken and changing the rules so it works better for more people.
vocabulary.example: Child labor reform meant new laws that took kids out of factories and put them in schools
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A reform is a change made to fix a problem in society, usually through new laws or practices. Progressive reforms tackled unsafe food, child labor, and corrupt elections. Every reform starts the same way: someone decides a problem is fixable and gets to work.

vocabulary.definition: A rule made by government that controls how businesses or industries must operate
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The government setting rules for business — like a referee in a game. Before the Progressive Era there was almost no referee, and companies could sell rotten meat or lock factory doors with workers inside.
vocabulary.example: The Pure Food and Drug Act was a regulation that forced companies to label products honestly and stop selling contaminated food
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A regulation is a government rule that controls how businesses must operate. Progressive Era regulations set standards for food safety, working conditions, and honest labeling. The debate over how much government should regulate business is still going strong today.

vocabulary.definition: The right to vote in political elections
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: One word, one meaning: the vote. When people fought for suffrage, they were fighting for the most basic tool of power in a democracy — a say in who makes the rules.
vocabulary.example: Women fought for suffrage for more than seventy years before the 19th Amendment finally guaranteed it in 1920
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Suffrage is the right to vote in political elections. For most of American history, that right was denied to most Americans, including all women. The fight for suffrage is one of the longest and most successful movements in the nation's story.

vocabulary.definition: The 1848 gathering in Seneca Falls, New York, that launched the organized women's rights movement in the United States
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The starting gun. About three hundred people met in a small New York town and publicly declared that women deserved equal rights — including, most radically, the vote. It took 72 more years, but it started here.
vocabulary.example: Elizabeth Cady Stanton helped organize the Seneca Falls Convention and drafted its Declaration of Sentiments
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 launched the organized women's rights movement in America. Organizers like Elizabeth Cady Stanton demanded equality, including the right to vote. It proves a lesson every movement learns: big change often starts with a small meeting.

vocabulary.definition: The document from the Seneca Falls Convention, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, declaring that women are equal to men and demanding their rights
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The Seneca Falls organizers took America's founding document and rewrote it: 'all men and women are created equal.' Using the nation's own words against its unfairness — that's a strategy movements have copied ever since.
vocabulary.example: The Declaration of Sentiments listed women's grievances the way the Declaration of Independence listed complaints against the king
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Declaration of Sentiments was written at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848. It copied the Declaration of Independence on purpose, declaring that all men and women are created equal. Holding a country to its own founding promises became a classic move in American reform.

vocabulary.definition: The constitutional amendment, ratified in 1920, that bars the United States and the states from denying the right to vote based on sex
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The finish line of the suffrage marathon. After 72 years of conventions, petitions, parades, and arrests, the Constitution finally said the vote could not be denied because of sex.
vocabulary.example: After the 19th Amendment was ratified in 1920, millions of American women voted in a presidential election for the first time
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, bars the government from denying the vote based on sex. It came 72 years after the Seneca Falls Convention first demanded it. Movements measure their work in decades, not days, and this one finally won.

vocabulary.definition: A large group of people working together over time to bring about social or political change
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: One person with a cause is a voice. Thousands of people, organized and persistent, are a movement — and movements are how everyday people have changed history without holding office.
vocabulary.example: The suffrage movement connected millions of people through local clubs, national organizations, marches, and publications
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A movement is a large group of people working together over time for social or political change. Movements succeed through organization, persistence, and strategy, not just passion. Studying how they operate reveals how everyday people have changed history.

vocabulary.definition: Describing change that is built from the bottom up by ordinary people in their own communities, rather than directed by the powerful
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Change that grows like grass — from the ground, not from the top. Neighbors organizing neighbors, one kitchen table and one community meeting at a time.
vocabulary.example: Suffrage was a grassroots effort for decades, with local women's clubs gathering signatures town by town
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Grassroots change is built from the bottom up by ordinary people in their communities. Instead of waiting for leaders to act, grassroots organizers recruit neighbors, hold meetings, and build pressure locally. Most major American reforms started exactly this way.

vocabulary.definition: A formal written request, usually signed by many people, asking a government or authority to take action
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A demand with receipts. One signature is an opinion; ten thousand signatures are proof that the public wants action — and the First Amendment protects your right to deliver them.
vocabulary.example: Suffragists delivered petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatures to Congress demanding a voting rights amendment
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A petition is a formal written request, signed by many people, asking those in power to act. The right to petition the government is protected by the First Amendment. Petitions turn scattered individual opinions into visible public pressure.

vocabulary.definition: Publicly supporting a cause and working to persuade others, especially decision-makers, to act on it
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Speaking up for something on purpose, with a plan. Advocacy is the everyday work of change: writing, calling, testifying, posting, and persuading — aimed at the people who can actually do something.
vocabulary.example: Jane Addams's advocacy for immigrant families included publishing articles, lobbying lawmakers, and speaking across the country
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Advocacy means publicly supporting a cause and persuading others to act on it. Effective advocates aim their message at people with the power to make the change they want. Your Civic Action Product is an act of advocacy aimed at a real audience.

vocabulary.definition: An alliance of different groups or organizations that join forces to reach a shared goal
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Movements rarely win alone. A coalition is when groups that don't agree on everything team up on the one thing they do agree on — because a bigger 'we' is harder to ignore.
vocabulary.example: The suffrage coalition included labor unions, temperance groups, and civil rights organizations working toward the same amendment
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A coalition is an alliance of different groups joining forces for a shared goal. Groups in a coalition may disagree on many things but unite on one. Progressive reformers won their biggest victories when many organizations pushed together.

vocabulary.definition: Steps a person or group takes to influence a public issue in their community, state, or nation
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Democracy is not a spectator sport. Civic action is anything you do to move a public issue — voting, organizing, speaking, creating, volunteering. This unit, you take yours.
vocabulary.example: Writing to a member of Congress, organizing a food drive, and making a documentary about an issue are all forms of civic action
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Civic action is any step a person takes to influence a public issue in their community or nation. It ranges from voting and petitioning to organizing, creating, and speaking out. The reformers we studied were everyday people who chose to act, and now it is your turn.

vocabulary.definition: A clear, debatable statement about an issue that you support with evidence
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Your product's backbone. A claim isn't a topic ('school lunch') or a fact ('lunch costs $3.50') — it's a position someone could argue against, which you then back up until they can't.
vocabulary.example: A strong claim: 'Congress should expand free school meals because hungry students cannot learn' — debatable, specific, and backed by evidence
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A claim is a clear, debatable statement that you support with evidence. It is a position someone could argue against, not just a topic or a fact. Your Civic Action Product stands or falls on the strength of its claim and the evidence behind it.

vocabulary.definition: The specific people a message or product is designed to reach and persuade, especially those with the power to act
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The muckrakers didn't write for everyone — they wrote for voters who could demand change. Knowing exactly who you're trying to move, and what moves them, is half the battle.
vocabulary.example: A letter about a national issue might target your representative, while a poster campaign targets classmates who can join the cause
vocabulary.typingSnippet: An audience is the specific group of people a message is designed to reach and persuade. Effective civic action targets an audience with the power to act on the issue. Every choice in your product, from format to tone, should fit the audience you picked.

vocabulary.definition: An official plan or course of action adopted by a government or organization to address an issue
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The 'what should actually happen' part. Reformers don't just name problems — they propose policies: specific rules, laws, or plans that would fix them. Your product should point toward one too.
vocabulary.example: The Pure Food and Drug Act turned public anger about unsafe food into an actual policy with inspections and penalties
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A policy is an official plan or course of action adopted by a government or organization. Movements succeed when they turn public anger into specific policy, the way muckraker outrage became food safety law. Strong civic action names the policy change it wants.

timelineEvents.title: Seneca Falls Convention
timelineEvents.description: The early root: decades before the Progressive Era, the organized women's rights movement begins in New York

timelineEvents.title: Hull House Founded
timelineEvents.description: Jane Addams opens a settlement house in Chicago serving immigrant families and training a generation of reformers

timelineEvents.title: How the Other Half Lives Published
timelineEvents.description: Jacob Riis's photographs of New York tenement life shock the public and spur housing reform

timelineEvents.title: NAWSA Formed
timelineEvents.description: Rival suffrage organizations merge into the National American Woman Suffrage Association, uniting the movement

timelineEvents.title: The Jungle Published
timelineEvents.description: Upton Sinclair's novel exposes the meatpacking industry and turns public stomachs into public pressure

timelineEvents.title: Pure Food and Drug Act
timelineEvents.description: Congress responds to muckraker outrage with landmark food and medicine safety regulation

timelineEvents.title: NAACP Founded
timelineEvents.description: Black and white activists, including Ida B. Wells and W. E. B. Du Bois, organize to fight for civil rights

timelineEvents.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Fire Spurs Reform
timelineEvents.description: Public grief over 146 deaths becomes organized pressure, winning dozens of new workplace safety laws

timelineEvents.title: Woman Suffrage Parade in Washington
timelineEvents.description: Thousands march on Pennsylvania Avenue the day before Wilson's inauguration, putting suffrage on the front page

timelineEvents.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
timelineEvents.description: Seventy-two years after Seneca Falls, the Constitution guarantees that the vote cannot be denied based on sex
